lead: A loop repeats a block of statements so you do not copy them by hand. A while loop repeats while a condition stays True. A for loop repeats once for each item in an iterable such as a range, a string or a list. Loops exist because a program often meets a list whose length is unknown while the code is being written, and because repeating one step over many items is the heart of almost every useful program. Uses: retrying a UPI PIN, printing a marks table for a class, adding a canteen bill until the last item, and drawing rows and columns of a pattern.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for boolean conditions and the if statement, and Unit 1 for range, integer arithmetic and indentation.

sections.h3: while: repeat while the condition is true

blocks.text: A while loop runs its body again and again as long as a boolean condition stays True. The condition sits at the top, so Python tests it before every pass, including the first one. If that first test is False, the body runs zero times.
The shape is the keyword while, a condition, a colon, then an indented body. Every line indented under the while line belongs to the loop.

blocks.code:
total = 0
i = 1
while i <= 5:
    total = total + i
    i = i + 1
print("sum =", total)
print("i after loop =", i)

blocks.text: At the end of the body, control jumps back to the condition. The body must change something the condition depends on. Here i = i + 1 moves i towards 6, so the test i <= 5 finally fails and the loop stops.

items: Evaluate the condition. It is either True or False.
If it is False, leave the loop and run the first statement after it.
If it is True, run the whole indented body once.

blocks.text: A sentinel-controlled loop stops on a special value rather than on a count. A canteen bill keeps adding amounts until the cashier enters the sentinel -1. The sentinel is read but never added to the total; it only ends the loop.

sections.h3: for: once for each item in an iterable

blocks.text: A for loop takes each item from an iterable and runs the body once per item. It stops by itself when the items run out, so no manual update is needed. Some syllabi call this definite iteration, because the number of passes is fixed before the loop starts, and they call the while loop indefinite iteration.

range(stop) gives 0, 1, ..., stop-1. range(start, stop) gives start up to stop-1. range(start, stop, step) jumps by step and stops before reaching stop. So range(1, 6) gives 1 2 3 4 5 — the 6 is never produced, and a negative step counts downwards.

blocks.where: N is how many values range(a, b, s) produces; a is the first value, b the stop value (excluded), s the step (positive). Example: range(3, 20, 4) gives N = ceiling(17 / 4) = ceiling(4.25) = 5 values. If b ≤ a with a positive step, range(a, b, s) is empty, so N = 0.

blocks.code:
word = "CHENNAI"
vowels = 0
for ch in word:
    if ch in "AEIOU":
        vowels = vowels + 1
print(vowels)
print(list(range(1, 10, 3)))

blocks.text: Over a string the loop variable takes one character per pass; over a list it takes one element per pass. No index arithmetic is needed. The block above also shows the accumulator pattern: a variable vowels is set to 0 before the loop, and each pass adds to it. The same pattern computes a total (total = total + x) or a count (count = count + 1).

A nested loop is a loop written inside another loop's body. The outer loop takes one step; then the inner loop runs completely, from its first item to its last. Next the outer loop takes its second step and the inner loop starts again from the beginning.
If the outer loop runs m times and the inner loop runs n times for each outer pass, the inner body runs m × n times in all. That product is the number the examiner usually asks for.

items: Row and column work: a marks table, a calendar grid, a picture of stars.
Grid coordinates: every pixel column for every pixel row.
Comparing every pair of items once, which costs about n² steps for n items.
A break inside the inner body leaves only the inner loop; the outer loop continues (see Chapter 2.3).

figure.caption: The test i ≤ 5 sits at the top and is checked before every pass; the dashed edge is the jump back. After the fifth pass i becomes 6, the test fails, and 15 is printed.

spec.title: while loop for sum 1 to 5
spec.aria: Flowchart adds 1 to 5 while i ≤ 5, then prints 15.

examples.question: The numbers starting at 3, increasing by 4, and staying below 20 are 3, 7, 11, 15, 19. Write a while loop that adds them and counts them. State the sum, the number of terms, and rewrite the loop as a for loop over range.
steps: Set total = 0, count = 0, i = 3 before the loop.
Test 23 < 20: False. Leave the loop with total = 55 and count = 5.
Match with range: range(3, 20, 4) produces 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, so the for loop runs the same five passes and gives the same sum 55.
examples.answer: The sum is 55 and the loop runs 5 times.
examples.check:
total = 0
count = 0
i = 3
while i < 20:
    total = total + i
    count = count + 1
    i = i + 4
print(total)
print(count)

examples.question: How many lines does this print, and what are they? for i in range(1, 4): for j in range(1, i + 1): print(i, j)
steps: Outer i = 1: inner range(1, 2) gives 1, so one line: 1 1.
Outer i = 2: inner range(1, 3) gives 1, 2, so two lines: 2 1 and 2 2.
Outer i = 3: inner range(1, 4) gives 1, 2, 3, so three lines: 3 1, 3 2, 3 3.

traps: Forgetting i = i + 1 inside a while loop. The condition never changes, so the program hangs with no error message.
Off-by-one: range(1, 6) gives 1 to 5, not 1 to 6. range(6) starts at 0. Read the start and the stop before you count passes.
break inside a nested loop leaves only the innermost loop; the outer loop runs its next pass normally.
Assigning to the loop variable inside a for body does not change the items the loop will visit next; for resets it from the iterable each pass.
Writing while i = 5 instead of while i == 5, or forgetting the colon and indentation, gives a syntax error before the loop even starts.

quiz.q: What numbers does range(2, 11, 3) produce, and how many are there?
quiz.a: 2, 5, 8 — three numbers. The next value, 11, equals the stop value and is excluded.

quiz.q: Why must a while loop body usually change the variable used in its condition?
quiz.a: The condition is re-tested before every pass. If nothing in the body can make it False, the test stays True and the loop never ends.

quiz.q: How many times does print(i, j) run in: for i in range(1, 5): for j in range(i): print(i, j)
quiz.a: range(i) has i items, so the inner body runs 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 times.

quiz.q: Give the final value of total: total = 0 for x in range(1, 10): total = total + x
i = 10 while i > 0: print(i) i = i - 3 Which numbers print, and which is last?
quiz.a: 10, 7, 4, 1 — four numbers, last is 1. Next i = -2, so -2 > 0 is False and the loop ends.

quiz.q: An outer loop runs over range(4) and an inner loop over range(3). A break fires during the second pass of the inner body. Which loop does it exit, and how many inner passes happen in total?
quiz.a: break exits only the inner loop. Each of the 4 outer passes runs the inner body twice (first pass, then break on the second), so 4 × 2 = 8 inner passes; the outer loop still runs 4 times.

quiz.q: Some syllabi call the for loop definite iteration and the while loop indefinite iteration. Explain the difference in one line.
quiz.a: A for loop's number of passes is fixed by the iterable before it starts; a while loop's number of passes depends on how long the condition stays True.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real code rarely counts to five; it walks files, database rows or network replies, which is why the for loop over an iterable matters more than the counting while loop. Unit 4 covers iterators and generators, where a loop is replaced by values produced on demand. The standard library's itertools module supplies ready-made loop patterns such as chaining and grouping. A server's main loop is usually while True with an exit path inside. Search for 'python itertools', 'generator expression' and 'enumerate and zip' next.
